column1: # Golden corpus for the ingredient parser — item 4 of docs/shopping-parser.md.
# Tab-separated:  line <TAB> quantity <TAB> unit <TAB> name <TAB> qualifier
# An empty unit or qualifier is an empty field. Blank lines and # are ignored.
# A line starting with ~ is a KNOWN GAP: the expectation is what the parser
# *should* produce, and it currently doesn't. The test asserts these still
# fail, so fixing one tells you to promote it rather than passing silently.
# Adding a case is one line. That is the whole point — every other item on
# the list is a heuristic, and heuristics regress each other.
# --- fractions, unicode and ascii, and ranges -----------------------------
# --- a size hyphenated onto the amount -------------------------------------
# Found by the novelty metric, which flagged "-inch piece" and "-and-half" as
# unrecognized ingredients — they were broken parses wearing a name.
# The size is unhyphenated here, and the shelf-word is "container" — which was
# not in the unit list, so the whole tail stayed in the name. You take one
# container off the shelf, which is the same reason "2 28-ounce cans" is 2 cans.
1 16 ounce container of fresh raw oysters in liquid
1 (15 oz) can black beans, drained and rinsed
# --- the same amount restated, without the parentheses (item 5) -----------
# --- the garlic family, which people write four ways ----------------------
# --- descriptors that should not survive into the name --------------------
# --- descriptors that are part of the identity and must survive -----------
# ...and the same words behaving as ordinary descriptors elsewhere.
# --- alternatives (item 6) — first option wins, rest becomes a note --------
2 tbsp olive oil or vegetable oil
# Same system on both sides, so item 5 correctly reads it as a choice rather
# than a conversion, and item 6 takes the first option.
1 lb chicken thighs or 2 lb beef
# --- amounts written across two units, and open-ended ones -----------------
# Found by the benchmark, not by anyone hitting them. "plus" is how a recipe
# writes an amount that doesn't divide neatly; the two are summed into the unit
2 cups flour plus more for dusting
# A range written with "or" rather than a dash.
# --- alternations that share a head noun -----------------------------------
# The first "option" is only an adjective, so splitting naively named the row
# ...against the identical shape that really is two ingredients, where the
# first option is a product in its own right and "butter oil" is not.
# ...and the one where neither reading is safe, so the phrase is kept whole.
# --- names that merely contain the letters "or" ----------------------------
# --- a step wearing an ingredient's clothes (item 7) -----------------------
1 tablespoon of all purpose flour dissolve in 1/4 cup water
2 tbsp cornstarch dissolved in 2 tbsp water
1 cup water combine with the cornstarch
1 cup rice rinse until the water runs clear
# --- how much it comes to once it's prepared -------------------------------
# "to yield 1 tablespoon" restates the amount after chopping. You buy the two
# sprigs, so the count on the row is already right and the clause is a note.
# Left in the name it also fed readTrailingUnit the *yield's* unit: the ginger
# line below used to come out measured in tablespoons with no amount at all.
2 sprigs fresh oregano to yield 1 tablespoon chopped
1 small red onion to yield 1/4 cup chopped
6 or 7 sprigs marjoram to make about 2 teaspoons finely chopped
1 bunch parsley to equal 1/2 cup chopped
Fresh ginger to yield 1 tablespoon, coarsely grated
# "Enough" is a hedge, not a name. Without stripping it, the alternation below
# read as two two-word options and confidently kept "enough fresh".
Enough fresh or frozen ginger to yield 1 tablespoon grated
# No amount after the clause means it says what the flour is *for*, not how
# much it comes to. Cutting there would cut the point of the line.
1 tablespoon flour to make a roux
# --- verbs that are part of a name and must survive ------------------------
# "chopped" is only stripped when it leads, so this keeps it. That's a
# normalize question (item 8), not an item 7 one — what matters here is that
# "chopped" did NOT get read as an instruction and take the spinach with it.
1 package frozen chopped spinach, thawed and squeezed dry
# A verb with no connective after it is naming a product, not giving a step.
# ...and when it is a step, the word that introduced it goes too.
1 tbsp olive oil to drizzle on top
# The count belongs to the fruit: you buy one lemon to get its juice.
# KNOWN GAPS — the expectation is right, the parser isn't there yet.
# Two ingredients on one line. Splitting them is its own change.
# "Salt and pepper to taste" is not here any more, and not because it was
# forgotten: two ingredients on one line are split by parseIngredientLines,
# which this file cannot express — every row here is one line in, one parse
# A "plus" after the name is the same shape and is still a gap: the second
# The same amount stated twice with nothing between the two — what a recipe
# plugin emits when the page shows both units ("1 stick" in black, "1/2 cup of
# butter" in grey) and the JSON-LD flattens them into one string.
# This is a gap on purpose, not an oversight. The shape is exactly the shape of
#     1 pound 2 ounces ground beef   — 1 lb PLUS 2 oz, one and a bit pounds
#     1 stick 1/2 cup of butter      — 1 stick IS 1/2 cup, one amount twice
# Nothing structural separates them, and `stick` is deliberately non-convertible
# (a cinnamon stick is not half a cup), so no conversion test can settle it
# either. 23 lines in 179,000 have this shape. Guessing would turn a correct
# "1 lb 2 oz" into a wrong one to fix a rarer case, which is the wrong trade —
# the row draws an invariant flag as it is, and "This is wrong" fixes it for
